questions.problem: A $2\times 3$ matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto an ellipse in ${R}^{2}.$ Given that the eigenvalues of ${A}^{T}A$ are $11,$ $9,$ and $0,$ find the length of the ellipse's semi-major axis.
questions.worked_solution:
The matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto the ellipse $\{Ax\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ in ${R}^{2}.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $Ax$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where ${x}^{T}({A}^{T}A)x$ is the quadratic form with the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$

Since the largest eigenvalue of ${A}^{T}A$ is $11,$ we obtain

$$
{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax{‖}^{2}\}=11\,⟹\,{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax‖\}=\sqrt{11}.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is $\sqrt{11}.$

questions.problem:
$$
R\,\bbox[5px,border:1px solid black]{\phantom{A}}={Q}^{T}\,\bbox[5px,border:1px solid black]{\phantom{A}}
$$

Let $A=QR$  be a QR decomposition of an $m\times n$ matrix $A$ with linearly independent columns, and the matrix equation above gives the least-squares solution of $Ax=b.$ From left to right, what are the missing parts of the equation?
questions.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the normal equation

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b.
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Finally, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ R\,\,x & ={Q}^{T}\,\,b.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the missing parts of the equation are $x$ and $b.$

questions.problem: Find the orthogonal projection matrix that maps $x\in {R}^{2}$ onto the subspace spanned by an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-1$ of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

Moreover, ${u}_{i}\cdot {u}_{i}^{T}$ is the projection matrix corresponding to ${u}_{i}.$

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda =-1.$ Computing $A-(-1)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A+1I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]+1[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations which is already in row echelon form and has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=0.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖v‖=1.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: 

$$
u=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {u}^{T} & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the following set of polynomials:

$$
{p}_{1}(t)=t-1,\,{p}_{2}(t)=2t+2,\,{p}_{3}(t)=2-2t.
$$

Given that the inner product in the vector space ${R}_{1}[t]$ of polynomials of degree at most $1$ in the variable $t$ is defined as 

$$
⟨p(t),q(t)⟩=p(-1)q(-1)+p(1)q(1),
$$

which of the following statements are true?

I. ${p}_{1}(t)⊥̸{p}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

II. ${p}_{2}(t)⊥{p}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

III. $S=\{{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t),{p}_{3}(t)\}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false since

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)⟩ & =⟨t-1,2t+2⟩ \\  & =(t-1){|}_{-1}\cdot (2t+2){|}_{-1}+(t-1){|}_{1}\cdot (2t+2){|}_{1} \\  & =((-1)-1)\cdot (2(-1)+2)+(1-1)\cdot (2(1)+2) \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{2}(t),{p}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨2t+2,2-2t⟩ \\  & =(2t+2){|}_{-1}\cdot (2-2t){|}_{-1}+(2t+2){|}_{1}\cdot (2-2t){|}_{1} \\  & =(2(-1)+2)\cdot (2-2(-1))+(2(1)+2)\cdot (2-2(1)) \\  & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${p}_{2}(t)⊥{p}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

- Statement III is false. Let's check if ${p}_{1}(t)⊥{p}_{3}(t).$ Computing the inner product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{3}(t)⟩ & =⟨t-1,2-2t⟩ \\  & =(t-1){|}_{-1}\cdot (2-2t){|}_{-1}+(t-1){|}_{1}\cdot (2-2t){|}_{1} \\  & =((-1)-1)\cdot (2-2(-1))+(1-1)\cdot (2-2(1)) \\  & =-8\ne 0,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that ${p}_{1}(t)⊥̸{p}_{3}(t)$ with respect to the given inner product. So, the set $S$ is *not* an orthogonal set.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

questions.problem:
The linear transformation $T$ has the standard matrix 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

 
What are the respective images of the standard basis vectors $\{i,j\}$ of ${R}^{2}$ under the action of $T?$
questions.worked_solution:
**Method 1**

The images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{i,j\}$ are the first and second columns of $T,$ respectively. 

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

We can find the images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{i,j\}$ by computing the matrix products $T\cdot i$ and $T\cdot j:$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T\cdot i=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T\cdot j=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Let $V=C[-1,1],$ the vector space of continuous functions over $[-1,1]$, and let the inner product on $V$ be defined as

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{-1}^{1}x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Now consider the following elements of $V:$ 

$$
{f}_{1}(t)=3t,\,{f}_{2}(t)={t}^{2}+1,\,g(t)=10{t}^{3}
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $S=\text{Span}\{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)\}$ given that ${f}_{1}(t)⊥{f}_{2}(t)$ with respect to the inner product, and that the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\text{Span}\{{f}_{1}(t)\}$ equals $6t.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the set $\{{f}_{1}(t),{f}_{2}(t)\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t)={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t).
$$

We are given that ${\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)=6t,$ so let's now find the orthogonal projection of $g(t)$ onto $\text{Span}\{{f}_{2}(t)\}.$ This can be computed as

$$
{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t)=\frac{⟨g(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}{⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}\,{f}_{2}(t).
$$

 

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨g(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}g(t){f}_{2}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}10{t}^{3}\cdot ({t}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}10{t}^{3}({t}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $10{t}^{3}$ is an odd function, while ${t}^{2}+1$ is even. Hence, their product $10{t}^{3}({t}^{2}+1)$ must be an odd function. Now, since we have an integral over the interval $[-1,1],$ which is symmetric about the origin, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-1}^{1}10{t}^{3}({t}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}t=0.
$$

  

Therefore,

$$
{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t)=\frac{0}{⟨{f}_{2}(t),{f}_{2}(t)⟩}\cdot ({t}^{2}+1)=0.
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,g(t) & ={\text{proj}}_{{f}_{1}(t)}\,g(t)+{\text{proj}}_{{f}_{2}(t)}\,g(t) \\  & =6t+0 \\  & =6t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the intersection point of the line $l$ and the plane $Π$ with equations

$$
l:r=⟨-2,1,4⟩+t⟨3,2,-6⟩,\,Π:-4x+3y-z-11=0.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's start by writing the equation of the line as

$$
r=⟨-2+3t,1+2t,4-6t⟩.
$$

Let's also write the equation of the plane in the dot product form:

$$
\begin{aligned}-4x+3y-z-11 & =0 \\ -4x+3y-z & =11 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨-4,3,-1⟩ & =11 \\ r\cdot ⟨-4,3,-1⟩ & =11\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $r=⟨-2+3t,1+2t,4-6t⟩$ into the equation of the plane, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot ⟨-4,3,-1⟩ & =11 \\ ⟨-2+3t,1+2t,4-6t⟩\cdot ⟨-4,3,-1⟩ & =11 \\ -4(-2+3t)+3(1+2t)-(4-6t) & =11 \\ 8-12t+3+6t-4+6t & =11 \\ 7 & =11.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation has no solution. Therefore, we conclude that the line $l$ and the plane $Π$ do not intersect.
